--- title: "Assignment 3: Verify the Claim" subtitle: "Analyzing ACS data with R" author: "Nathan Leroy" date: today format: html: toc: true code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" embed-resources: true execute: warning: false message: false editor: markdown: wrap: 72 --- This analysis attempts to measure the accuracy of a 2018 article by the Philadelphia Media Network, "[New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty](https://whyy.org/articles/new-census-figures-on-philly-neighborhoods-show-inequality-high-numbers-of-whites-living-in-poverty/)". This article uses American Community Survey (ACS) data to conduct a neighborhood-by-neighborhood analysis of poverty and demographic conditions across Philadelphia. According to the article, conditions in Philadelphia have gotten increasingly worse over the last 2 decades, with the following examples as proof: - Poverty rates in the neighborhood of Eastwick increased from 12 to 26 percent between the 2006-10 census and the 2013-17 census. - The median household income of Tioga-Nicetown declined from \$28,026 to \$17,493. - White poverty increased drastically throughout the city, with the neighborhood of Holmesburg showing an over 900 percent increase (2% to 19%). - The neighborhood of Fairhill had a poverty rate of 61 percent, and its median income dropped by \$300. - Visualizations of changes in poverty rates in Philadelphia show a significant increase in many of the poorer areas of the city. The purpose of this analysis is to verify some of the claims made in the article by reconstructing the analysis of the ACS data and testing if the reported changes in the article are statistically significant. ## Part 1: Import Data & Create Tables First, we install all required packages. An API key from the US Census Bureau is required for this project, and it needs to be installed before any data can be fetched. A key can be easily obtained [here](https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Install required packages library(tidycensus) library(tidyverse) ``` ::: After installing all the packages and confirming the API key is set up, we can start importing data from the ACS table. For this analysis, we will use the following codes: - B17001_001: total population of an area for which poverty can be determined. - B17001_002: total number of people in that area who fall below the poverty line. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Variables from ACS table: total in poverty and total below poverty_vars <- c( total_poverty = "B17001_001", below_poverty = "B17001_002" ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates #| message: false #| warning: false poverty_2013_2017 <- get_acs( geography = "tract", variables = poverty_vars, state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia", year = 2017, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", moe_level = 90 ) poverty_2013_2017 <- poverty_2013_2017 %>% mutate( period = "2013–2017", poverty_rate = (below_povertyE / total_povertyE) * 100 ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 2006–2010 ACS 5-year estimates #| message: false #| warning: false poverty_2006_2010 <- get_acs( geography = "tract", variables = poverty_vars, state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia", year = 2010, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", moe_level = 90 ) poverty_2006_2010 <- poverty_2006_2010 %>% mutate( period = "2006–2010", poverty_rate = (below_povertyE / total_povertyE) * 100 ) ``` ::: Here, we combine the data from each census into a single table for easier analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_both <- bind_rows( poverty_2006_2010, poverty_2013_2017 ) %>% select( GEOID, NAME, period, total_povertyE, total_povertyM, below_povertyE, below_povertyM, poverty_rate ) %>% arrange(GEOID, period) poverty_both ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 768 × 8 GEOID NAME period total_povertyE total_povertyM below_povertyE 1 42101000100 Census Tract… 2006–… 3042 455 364 2 42101000100 Census Tract… 2013–… 4155 429 292 3 42101000200 Census Tract… 2006–… 1919 270 138 4 42101000200 Census Tract… 2013–… 2558 425 962 5 42101000300 Census Tract… 2006–… 2915 315 271 6 42101000300 Census Tract… 2013–… 3315 311 280 7 42101000401 Census Tract… 2006–… 1525 277 529 8 42101000401 Census Tract… 2013–… 2632 287 486 9 42101000402 Census Tract… 2006–… 3156 302 263 10 42101000402 Census Tract… 2013–… 3299 419 141 # ℹ 758 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: below_povertyM , poverty_rate ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_change <- poverty_both %>% select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate) %>% pivot_wider( names_from = period, values_from = poverty_rate ) %>% mutate( change_percentage_points = `2013–2017` - `2006–2010` ) %>% arrange(desc(change_percentage_points)) # View the tracts with the largest increases poverty_change %>% select( GEOID, NAME, `2006–2010`, `2013–2017`, change_percentage_points ) %>% print(n = 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 384 × 5 GEOID NAME `2006–2010` `2013–2017` change_percentage_po…¹ 1 42101005600 Census Tract 56, … 13.1 48.8 35.7 2 42101006000 Census Tract 60, … 4.05 34.9 30.9 3 42101000200 Census Tract 2, P… 7.19 37.6 30.4 4 42101020000 Census Tract 200,… 30.6 58.5 27.9 5 42101030502 Census Tract 305.… 5.31 31.5 26.2 6 42101989100 Census Tract 9891… 69.1 92.5 23.3 7 42101038900 Census Tract 389,… 13.4 35.3 21.8 8 42101016701 Census Tract 167.… 27.6 48.3 20.7 9 42101024500 Census Tract 245,… 38.5 59.0 20.4 10 42101029100 Census Tract 291,… 27.4 46.7 19.3 11 42101020300 Census Tract 203,… 27.4 46.2 18.8 12 42101011000 Census Tract 110,… 29.7 48.2 18.4 13 42101010600 Census Tract 106,… 26.4 44.7 18.3 14 42101017602 Census Tract 176.… 44.0 61.6 17.6 15 42101029000 Census Tract 290,… 25.7 43.1 17.4 16 42101015101 Census Tract 151.… 34.3 50.7 16.4 17 42101024400 Census Tract 244,… 18.5 34.8 16.4 18 42101030100 Census Tract 301,… 19.9 35.8 15.9 19 42101008102 Census Tract 81.0… 19.1 34.7 15.6 20 42101033000 Census Tract 330,… 16.4 31.6 15.2 # ℹ 364 more rows # ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​change_percentage_points ``` ::: ::: ## Part 2: Testing In this portion of our analysis, we want to determine how reliable our data for each census tract is. First, we calculate the MOE of the poverty rate for each census. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate poverty rate and its MOE # 2006-2010 poverty_2006_2010 <- poverty_2006_2010 %>% mutate( poverty_rate = below_povertyE / total_povertyE, poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop( num = below_povertyE, denom = total_povertyE, moe_num = below_povertyM, moe_denom = total_povertyM ) ) # 2013-2017 poverty_2013_2017 <- poverty_2013_2017 %>% mutate( poverty_rate = below_povertyE / total_povertyE, poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop( num = below_povertyE, denom = total_povertyE, moe_num = below_povertyM, moe_denom = total_povertyM ) ) ``` ::: We also want to calculate the coefficient of variation. We can do this using the two formulas below: $$ SE = \frac{\text{MOE}}{1.645} $$ And: $$ CV = \frac{\text{SE}}{estimate} * 100 $$ We use the thresholds determined by Jurjevich et al. (2018) for this analysis: - CV \< 12% is reliable - CV \> 12% and CV \< 40% is somewhat reliable - CV \> 40% is unreliable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # CV Calculations poverty_2006_2010 <- poverty_2006_2010 %>% mutate( poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645, poverty_rate_cv = (poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate) * 100, reliability = case_when( poverty_rate_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable", poverty_rate_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable", poverty_rate_cv > 40 ~ "Unreliable", TRUE ~ NA_character_ ) ) poverty_2013_2017 <- poverty_2013_2017 %>% mutate( poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645, poverty_rate_cv = (poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate) * 100, reliability = case_when( poverty_rate_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable", poverty_rate_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable", poverty_rate_cv > 40 ~ "Unreliable", TRUE ~ NA_character_ ) ) ``` ::: After these calculations, we join the two periods together to create one dataset with one row per tract using an inner join. ::: callout-tip We use an inner join because we want tracts that have data in both periods for the change calculation. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_change <- poverty_2006_2010 %>% select( GEOID, NAME, poverty_rate_2006_2010 = poverty_rate, poverty_moe_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_moe, poverty_cv_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_cv, reliability_2006_2010 = reliability ) %>% inner_join( poverty_2013_2017 %>% select( GEOID, poverty_rate_2013_2017 = poverty_rate, poverty_moe_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_moe, poverty_cv_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_cv, reliability_2013_2017 = reliability ), by = "GEOID" ) ``` ::: Finally, we calculate the change in poverty rates by simply subtracting the 2006-10 rate from the newer 2013-17 rate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_change <- poverty_change %>% mutate( change = poverty_rate_2013_2017 - poverty_rate_2006_2010 ) # To make it easier to read, convert proportions into percents poverty_change <- poverty_change %>% mutate( change_percentage_points = change * 100 ) ``` ::: To calculate the MOE of the change between the two periods, we can use this formula: $$\text{MOE}_{\text{change}} = \sqrt{\text{MOE}_1^2 + \text{MOE}_2^2}$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_change <- poverty_change %>% mutate( change_moe = sqrt( poverty_moe_2006_2010^2 + poverty_moe_2013_2017^2 ) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_change <- poverty_change %>% mutate( change_lower = change - change_moe, change_upper = change + change_moe ) ``` ::: Now, we can check if the change is statistically significant at the 90% confidence interval. If the change is larger than the MOE we calculated earlier, the it is considered to be statistically significant. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_change <- poverty_change %>% mutate( change_significant = abs(change) > change_moe ) ``` ::: Several census tracts have missing or incomplete values. We can run the script below to identify all of these tracts before deciding what to do with them. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_change %>% filter( is.na(poverty_rate_2006_2010) | is.na(poverty_rate_2013_2017) | is.na(change) ) %>% select( GEOID, NAME, poverty_rate_2006_2010, poverty_rate_2013_2017, change ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 8 × 5 GEOID NAME poverty_rate_2006_2010 poverty_rate_2013_2017 change 1 42101005000 Census Tract… NaN NaN NaN 2 42101980300 Census Tract… NaN NaN NaN 3 42101980400 Census Tract… NaN NaN NaN 4 42101980500 Census Tract… NaN NaN NaN 5 42101980600 Census Tract… 0.0978 NaN NaN 6 42101980700 Census Tract… NaN NaN NaN 7 42101980800 Census Tract… NaN NaN NaN 8 42101980900 Census Tract… NaN NaN NaN ``` ::: ::: For this analysis, we will drop any incomplete rows, as the poverty level cannot be accurately calculated. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_analysis <- poverty_change %>% filter( !is.na(change), !is.na(change_moe), !is.na(change_significant) ) ``` ::: After the incomplete rows are dropped, we can calculate the total amount of tracts with a detectable change in poverty level. 63/313 (approximately 16.75 percent) of the tracts show a statistically significant change in poverty level. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_analysis %>% summarise( detectable_change = sum(change_significant), no_detectable_change = sum(!change_significant), total_tracts = n(), percent_detectable = mean(change_significant) * 100, percent_not_detectable = mean(!change_significant) * 100 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 detectable_change no_detectable_change total_tracts percent_detectable 1 63 313 376 16.8 # ℹ 1 more variable: percent_not_detectable ``` ::: ::: This table displays all the calculated data associated with the tracts. The tracts with the greatest change in poverty level are displayed on top. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_analysis %>% select( GEOID, NAME, poverty_rate_2006_2010, poverty_moe_2006_2010, poverty_rate_2013_2017, poverty_moe_2013_2017, change_percentage_points, change_moe, reliability_2006_2010, reliability_2013_2017, change_significant ) %>% arrange(desc(abs(change_percentage_points))) change_significant ``` ::: ::: ## Part 3: Results and Visualizations ### Map We haven't imported the geometry of the tracts yet, so we need to run the following code block: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #| include: false library(sf) invisible(capture.output( tracts <- get_acs( geography = "tract", variables = "B01003_001", state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia", year = 2017, survey = "acs5", geometry = TRUE ) )) ``` ::: Next, we join it to the main table. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_map <- tracts %>% select(GEOID, geometry) %>% left_join( poverty_analysis, by = "GEOID" ) ``` ::: Finally, we display the map. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_map %>% mutate( change_percentage_points = change * 100 ) %>% ggplot() + geom_sf( aes(fill = change_percentage_points), color = "black" ) + scale_fill_gradient2( name = "Change in poverty rate\n(percentage points)" ) + theme_void() + labs( title = "Change in Poverty Rates Across Philadelphia", subtitle = "Census tract ACS 5-year estimates, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017", caption = "Grey values indicate no data." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](assignment3_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: This map displays where there is a statistically significant change in poverty levels between the two censuses. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_map %>% mutate( change_status = case_when( change_significant & change > 0 ~ "Detectable increase", change_significant & change < 0 ~ "Detectable decrease", TRUE ~ "No detectable change" ) ) %>% ggplot() + geom_sf( aes(fill = change_status), color = "black", linewidth = 0.3 ) + theme_void() + labs( title = "Statistically Significant Changes in Philadelphia Poverty Rates", subtitle = "Census tract ACS 5-year estimates, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017", fill = "Change status", caption = "A detectable change falls outside of the 90% confidence interval." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](assignment3_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Errorbar Visualization This visualization shows only the statistically significant changes in poverty rates between the two time periods. The bars represent the estimated change, while the error bars (thinner black bars) represent the 90% margin of error. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} poverty_analysis %>% filter(change_significant) %>% arrange(change) %>% slice_head(n = 15) %>% ggplot(aes(x = reorder(GEOID, change), y = change * 100)) + geom_col(aes(fill = change > 0)) + geom_errorbar( aes( ymin = (change - change_moe) * 100, ymax = (change + change_moe) * 100 ), width = 0.3 ) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + coord_flip() + theme_minimal() + labs( title = "Statistically Significant Changes in Poverty Rates", subtitle = "Philadelphia census tracts, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017", x = "Census tract", y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)", caption = "Bars show estimated change; error bars show the 90% margin of error." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](assignment3_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Reliability Table This table displays the reliability of census tract poverty estimates based on their CV. Lower CV values indicate more reliable estimates. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Reliability table ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gt) reliability_table <- poverty_analysis %>% mutate( cv = pmax( poverty_cv_2006_2010, poverty_cv_2013_2017, na.rm = TRUE ), dot = case_when( cv < 12 ~ "🟢", cv <= 40 ~ "🟡", TRUE ~ "🔴" ), flag = case_when( cv < 12 ~ "Reliable", cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable", TRUE ~ "Unreliable" ) ) %>% arrange(desc(cv)) %>% select( dot, GEOID, poverty_cv_2006_2010, poverty_cv_2013_2017, flag ) reliability_table %>% gt() %>% fmt_number( columns = c(poverty_cv_2006_2010, poverty_cv_2013_2017), ) %>% cols_label( dot = "", GEOID = "Census tract", poverty_cv_2006_2010 = "CV (%)\n2006–2010", poverty_cv_2013_2017 = "CV (%)\n2013–2017", flag = "Reliability" ) %>% cols_align( align = "center", columns = dot ) %>% tab_header( title = "Reliability of Philadelphia Census Tract Poverty Estimates", subtitle = "ACS 5-year estimates, 2006–2010 and 2013–2017" ) %>% tab_source_note( "Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

::: ## Part 4: Adjudication of Claims A challenge of this project is that the census tracts found in the ACS dataset do not correspond to traditional boundaries of Philadelphia neighborhoods, which are somewhat informal and not collected or defined by the city for official use. Therefore, we have to estimate which tracts fall into the neighborhoods the article is analyzing. This process is naturally a source of error in this project. ![Philadelphia Neighborhood Maps - Revolve Philly Group \| Map ...](https://i.pinimg.com/736x/16/09/2d/16092d197f53e945fcdd5f2ad911574e.jpg){width="506"} The article particularly analyzes: - Fairhill (26): located in North Philadelphia; a predominantly white neighborhood. This registered the highest poverty rate in the city, 61 percent. This article explains how low-income neighborhoods are at particular risk of falling further into poverty, using Fairhill as an example. - Analysis: While the area around Fairhill did indeed see an average increase in poverty based on the map, few of these changes were statistically significant. Although the data does show that poverty increased slightly here, there is limited statistical evidence that poverty increased beyond the bounds of the variability of the ACS data. - Eastwick (10): located Southwest Philadelphia: a predominantly black and low-income neighborhood. This neighborhood showed the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community, going from 12 to 26 percent. - Analysis: From our map in part 3, there did not appear to be any statistically significant increases in poverty rate during the study period. In fact, some of the areas showed a statistically significant decrease in poverty rate. This contrasts with the claim of the article that the poverty rate has more than doubled in this area. Since all of our census tract data from Southwest Philadelphia shows either statistically significant decline in poverty or no statistically significant change, we can confidently refute this claim. - Holmesburg (50): located in Northeast Philadelphia: a predominantly white, working-class neighborhood. The article claims that poverty skyrocketed here, increasing more than 9x from 2 percent to 19 percent. - In the Northeast Philadelphia area, there is a mix of statistically significant increases in poverty, statistically significant decreases, and non-significant changes. It seems unlikely for a 9x increase in poverty to occur in an area around here, but since the neighborhood boundaries do not correspond exactly with the census tracts, we cannot confidently confirm or refute the claim specifically for Holmesburg. - Tioga-Nicetown (31): a predominantly black neighborhood located in Northwest Philadelphia: according to the article, the median income of this neighborhood dropped from 28,026 to 17,493, the largest drop in the city. - Analysis: in the census tract nearest to Tioga-Nicetown, a statistically significant increase in poverty can be observed. This corresponds with the 40 percent decrease in median income reported in the article. Areas bordering the neighborhood did not see statistically significant increases in poverty, however. The analysis in the article appears to be valid. ## Part 5: Conclusion Philadelphia continues to suffer from high poverty rates, particularly around minority-heavy areas in North Philly and West Philly. Income inequality is particularly high here, with statistically significant increases in wealth being observed between the 2010 and 2017 census. However, many lower-income areas in North Philly are seeing statistically significant decreases in poverty rates, which may suggest a sign of hope for these communities. Therefore, this analysis provides mixed evidence for the article's claims. Changes in poverty were not uniform across Philadelphia, and some areas in close proximity to each other experienced significant increases in poverty while some experienced significant decreases. Many other areas experienced no statistically significant changes at all. The data in many of these census tracts was deemed either "somewhat reliable" or "unreliable" based on its MOE, and a more detailed and complete survey of this area is necessary to get fully accurate results. Additionally, it would improve the accuracy of this analysis to conduct the survey by neighborhood instead of by census tract; however, it would be quite logistically challenging.
